items.t: Anti-inflammatory analgesic for rheumatoid arthritis (including Still's disease), osteoarthritis, and muscular, traumatic, dental, headache, post-operative and postpartum pain; pyrexia in children.

src.q: As an anti-inflammatory analgesic for the symptomatic relief of rheumatoid arthritis (including Still's Disease), osteoarthritis, and pain including muscular, traumatic and dental pain
headaches of most aetiology, post-operative and postpartum pain; pyrexia in children.

items.t: Primary dysmenorrhoea; menorrhagia due to dysfunctional causes or an IUD once other pelvic pathology is ruled out.

src.q: Primary dysmenorrhoea.
Menorrhagia due to dysfunctional causes and presence of an IUD when other pelvic pathology has been ruled out.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK SmPCs (two UK 250 mg capsule SmPCs) or the MHRA/SPS pages accessed.

items.t: Adults: 500 mg (2 capsules) three times daily. Do not exceed the stated dose; lowest effective dose for the shortest time.

src.q: Adults 2 capsules (500 mg) three times daily.
Do not exceed the stated dose.
Undesirable effects may be minimised by using the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration necessary to control symptoms

items.t: Menorrhagia: start on the first day of excessive bleeding. Dysmenorrhoea: start at the onset of menstrual pain. Continue as the physician judges.

src.q: In menorrhagia to be administered on the first day of excessive bleeding and continued according to the judgment of the physician.
In dysmenorrhoea to be administered at the onset of menstrual pain and continued according to the judgment of the physician.

items.t: Elderly (over 65): adult dose, but higher risk of serious adverse effects; lowest dose for the shortest time, monitor regularly for GI bleeding; caution with dehydration and renal disease.

src.q: Elderly (over 65 years) As for adults.
The patient should be monitored regularly for GI bleeding during NSAID therapy
should be used with caution in elderly patients suffering from dehydration and renal disease.

items.t: Under 12 years: one UK SmPC recommends the 50 mg/5 ml suspension instead of capsules; another UK capsule SmPC says not recommended under 12.

src.q: It is recommended that children under 12 years of age should be given Mefenamic Acid Suspension (50 mg / 5 ml).
Children (under 12 years): Not recommended.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to mefenamic acid or excipients; previous hypersensitivity (asthma, bronchospasm, rhinitis, angioedema, urticaria) to aspirin, ibuprofen or other NSAIDs.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
mefenamic acid must not be given to patients who have previously shown hypersensitivity reaction (e.g. asthma, bronchospasm, rhinitis, angioedema or urticaria) to these medicines.

items.t: Inflammatory bowel disease; history of GI bleeding or perforation related to previous NSAIDs; active or history of recurrent peptic ulcer/haemorrhage.

src.q: Inflammatory bowel disease.
History of gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, related to previous NSAIDs therapy.
Active, or history of recurrent peptic ulcer/haemorrhage (two or more distinct episodes of proven ulceration or bleeding).

items.t: Severe heart failure, hepatic failure, renal failure; last trimester of pregnancy; pain after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery.

src.q: Severe heart failure, hepatic failure and renal failure (see section 4.4).
During the last trimester of pregnancy (see section 4.6).
Treatment of pain after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery.

items.t: The generic capsule SmPC also lists intestinal ulceration and use with other NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors) in section 4.3; the originator SmPC lists other NSAIDs under warnings and interactions only.

src.q: intestinal ulceration and history of upper gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation
Use with concomitant NSAIDs including cyclo oxygenase 2 specific inhibitors (See section 4.5 Interactions).

items.t: GI bleeding, ulceration or perforation can occur at any time and can be fatal; risk rises with dose, ulcer history and age; smoking and alcohol add risk. Consider gastroprotection (misoprostol or a PPI) in those at risk. Withdraw if GI bleeding or ulceration occurs.

src.q: GI bleeding, ulceration or perforation, which can be fatal, has been reported with all NSAIDs at any time during treatment
Smoking and alcohol use are added risk factors.
Combination therapy with protective agents (e.g. misoprostol or proton pump inhibitors) should be considered for patients at risk of GI bleeding
When GI bleeding or ulceration occurs in patients receiving mefenamic acid the treatment should be withdrawn.

items.t: Cardiovascular: uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure, ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial or cerebrovascular disease only after careful consideration; a thrombotic risk cannot be excluded. Hypertension or mild to moderate heart failure needs monitoring and advice (fluid retention, oedema).

src.q: Patients with uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure, established ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, and/or cerebrovascular disease should only be treated with mefenamic acid after careful consideration.
There are insufficient data to exclude such a risk for mefenamic acid.
Appropriate monitoring and advice are required for patients with a history of hypertension and/or mild to moderate congestive heart failure

items.t: Renal: may precipitate renal failure; highest risk with renal, cardiac or liver impairment, diuretics and in the elderly; monitor renal function. Take precautions in dehydration and renal disease.

src.q: precipitate renal failure
Patients at greatest risk of this reaction are those with impaired renal function, cardiac impairment, liver dysfunction, those taking diuretics and the elderly.
Renal function should be monitored in these patients
Precaution should be taken in patients suffering from dehydration and renal disease, particularly the elderly.

items.t: Asthma (current or past): caution, bronchospasm possible. Intracranial haemorrhage or bleeding diathesis: use with caution (platelet effects). Epilepsy: caution.

src.q: Caution is required if administered to patients suffering from, or with a previous history of, bronchial asthma
they should be used in caution in patients with intracranial haemorrhage and bleeding diathesis
Caution should be exercised when treating patients suffering from epilepsy.

items.t: Diarrhoea: withdraw immediately and do not give mefenamic acid again (associated with proctocolitis). Prolonged therapy: watch for liver dysfunction, rash, blood dyscrasias or diarrhoea, and stop immediately if they appear.

src.q: If diarrhoea does develop the drug should be withdrawn immediately and this patient should not receive mefenamic acid again.
Patients on prolonged therapy should be kept under regular surveillance with particular attention to liver dysfunction, rash, blood dyscrasias or development of diarrhoea.
Appearance of any of these symptoms should be regarded as an indication to stop therapy immediately

items.t: Serious skin reactions (exfoliative dermatitis, SJS, TEN), mostly in the first month: stop at the first rash, mucosal lesion or sign of hypersensitivity.

src.q: Mefenamic acid should be stopped at the first appearance of skin rash, mucosal lesions or any other sign of hypersensitivity.

items.t: SLE / mixed connective tissue disease: possible increased risk of aseptic meningitis. Known or suspected poor CYP2C9 metabolisers: use with caution (raised plasma levels).

src.q: In patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and mixed connective tissue disorders there may be an increased risk of aseptic meningitis
In patients who are known or suspected to be poor CYP2C9 metabolisers based on previous history/experience with other CYP2C9 substrates, mefenamic acid should be administered with caution

items.t: Medication-overuse headache with prolonged use for headaches: stop treatment. Lactose: hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine. Lack of response in dysmenorrhoea or menorrhagia: look for other causes.

src.q: Prolonged use of any type of painkiller for headaches can make them worse.
Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
In dysmenorrhoea and menorrhagia lack of response should alert the physician to investigate other causes.

items.t: Anticoagulants such as warfarin: NSAIDs may enhance the effect; oral anticoagulants need careful prothrombin time monitoring; NSAIDs with warfarin or heparin are considered unsafe unless under direct medical supervision.

src.q: NSAIDs may enhance the effects of anti-coagulants, such as warfarin
Concurrent administration of mefenamic acid with oral anti-coagulant drugs requires careful prothrombin time monitoring.
It is considered unsafe to take NSAIDs in combination with warfarin or heparin unless under direct medical supervision.

items.t: Other NSAIDs, including aspirin and COX-2 inhibitors: avoid two or more together. Antiplatelets, SSRIs, corticosteroids: increased GI bleeding/ulceration risk; use with caution.

src.q: Avoid concomitant use of two or more NSAIDs (including aspirin) as this may increase the risk of adverse effects

Caution should be advised in patients receiving concomitant medications which could increase the risk of gastrotoxicity or bleeding such as corticosteroids, anticoagulants such as warfarin, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or anti-platelet agents such as aspirin

items.t: Low-dose aspirin: experimental data suggest mefenamic acid may interfere with its antiplatelet effect; no firm conclusion for regular use.

src.q: Experimental data implies that mefenamic acid interferes with the anti-platelet effect of low-dose aspirin when given concomitantly
no firm conclusions can be made for regular mefenamic acid use

items.t: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin-II receptor antagonists: reduced antihypertensive effect and risk of renal impairment (especially elderly); keep hydrated and assess renal function at the start and during use. Diuretics and antihypertensives: reduced effect; diuretics increase nephrotoxicity.

src.q: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin-II-receptor antagonists: A reduction in antihypertensive effect and an increased risk of renal impairment especially in elderly patients.
Patients should be adequately hydrated, and the renal function assessed in the beginning and during concomitant therapy.
Antihypertensives and diuretics: A reduction in antihypertensive and diuretic effect has been observed.
Diuretics can increase the nephrotoxicity of NSAIDs.

items.t: Sulfonylureas: inhibited metabolism, longer half-life, increased hypoglycaemia risk. Methotrexate: reduced elimination, higher levels. Quinolone antibiotics: possible increased convulsion risk. Aminoglycosides: reduced renal function and higher aminoglycoside levels.

src.q: Oral hypoglycaemic agents : Inhibition of metabolism of sulfonylurea drugs, prolonged half-life and increased risk of hypoglycaemia.
Methotrexate: Elimination of the drug can be reduced, resulting in increased plasma levels.
Patients taking NSAIDs and quinolones may have an increased risk of developing convulsions.
Aminoglycosides : Reduction in renal function in susceptible individuals, decreased elimination of aminoglycoside and increased plasma concentrations.

items.t: Others: lithium (raised levels; watch for toxicity), cardiac glycosides (raised levels, worse heart failure), ciclosporin and tacrolimus (nephrotoxicity), zidovudine (haematological toxicity), probenecid (reduced NSAID elimination), mifepristone (no NSAIDs for 8-12 days after), other plasma-protein-bound drugs (dose change may be needed).

src.q: Patients should be observed carefully for signs of lithium toxicity.
NSAIDs may exacerbate cardiac failure, reduce GFR and increase plasma cardiac glycoside levels.
The risk of nephrotoxicity of ciclosporin may be increased with NSAIDs.
Zidovudine: Increased risk of haematological toxicity when NSAIDs are given with zidovudine.
NSAIDs should not be taken for 8-12 days after mifepristone administration
Concurrent therapy with other plasma protein binding drugs may necessitate a modification in dosage.

items.t: Warfarin (warfarin SmPC): NSAIDs should be avoided, or given with caution and increased clinical and laboratory monitoring.

src.q: The following examples should be avoided, or administered with caution with increased clinical and laboratory monitoring
NSAIDs (including aspirin and cox-2 specific NSAIDS)

items.t: Spironolactone (spironolactone SmPC): NSAIDs such as mefenamic acid may reduce its diuretic effect; NSAIDs with spironolactone may lead to severe hyperkalaemia. ACE inhibitors (lisinopril SmPC): worsening renal function and raised potassium; caution, especially in the elderly. Metformin (metformin SmPC): close renal monitoring.

src.q: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as aspirin, indomethacin, and mefenamic acid may attenuate the natriuretic efficacy of diuretics
may lead to severe hyperkalaemia
The combination should be administered with caution, especially in the elderly.
When starting or using such products in combination with metformin, close monitoring of renal function is necessary.

items.t: Methotrexate (SPS, methotrexate SmPC): increased toxicity risk; use with caution on specialist advice; not recommended with any renal impairment.

src.q: Use NSAIDs in combination with methotrexate with caution on the advice of the specialist (for example, rheumatologist).
If risk factors such as renal function disorders, including mild renal impairment, are present, combined administration with NSAIDs is not recommended.

src.q: Severe heart failure, hepatic failure and renal failure (see section 4.4).

items.t: Last trimester: contraindicated (ductus arteriosus closure, fetal renal dysfunction, delayed labour, increased bleeding in mother and child).

src.q: use in the last trimester of pregnancy is contraindicated

systemic (oral and injectable) NSAIDs are contraindicated during the last trimester (after 28 weeks) of pregnancy

items.t: First and second trimesters and labour: should not be used unless benefit outweighs risk to the fetus; lowest dose, shortest time. From week 20: oligohydramnios and ductus arteriosus constriction possible; consider antenatal monitoring after several days; stop if found.

src.q: NSAIDs should not be used during the first two trimesters of pregnancy or labour unless the potential benefit to the patient outweighs the potential risk to the foetus.
From the 20th week of pregnancy onward, Mefenamic Acid use may cause oligohydramnios resulting from foetal renal dysfunction.
Antenatal monitoring for oligohydramnios and ductus arteriosus constriction should be considered
should be discontinued if oligohydramnios or ductus arteriosus constriction are found.

items.t: MHRA: avoid systemic NSAIDs from week 20 unless clinically required; lowest dose for the shortest time. SPS: ibuprofen is the preferred NSAID in pregnancy.

src.q: avoid prescribing systemic NSAIDs from week 20 of pregnancy unless clinically required and prescribe the lowest dose for the shortest time in these circumstances
Ibuprofen is the preferred NSAID in pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS: use in pregnancy is not advised unless prescribed by a doctor, especially from 20 weeks; paracetamol is usually recommended instead.

src.q: Use of mefenamic acid during pregnancy is not advised unless prescribed by a doctor, especially if you are 20 or more weeks pregnant.
Paracetamol is usually recommended to control pain or fever during pregnancy.

items.t: Originator SmPC: trace amounts may pass into milk; should not be taken by nursing mothers. Generic capsule SmPC: NSAIDs should, if possible, be avoided when breastfeeding.

src.q: Trace amounts of mefenamic acid may be present in breast milk and transmitted to the nursing infant.
Therefore, mefenamic acid should not be taken by nursing mothers.
NSAIDs should, if possible, be avoided when breastfeeding.
